title: Heirloom cobweb stole
subtitle: A rectangular stole in cobweb-weight yarn with a traditional Shetland spider lace pattern.
excerpt: A rectangular stole in cobweb-weight 1-ply Shetland-type wool worked in the traditional spider lace pattern. The cobweb weight creates an extraordinarily fine and translucent fabric. Finished size approximately 35 cm wide by 150 cm long, blocked. About 100 g of cobweb-weight yarn.
sourceNotes: Spider lace (sometimes called toad-in-a-puddle or ring lace) is a traditional Shetland lace pattern documented in Sarah Don, The Art of Shetland Lace (1980), §Stitches. The spider motif is a standard Shetland pattern with no single inventor; it appears in Victorian era Shetland knitting samples at the V&A Museum collections. Cobweb-weight construction is traditional for heirloom Shetland stoles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A traditional Shetland lace motif in which yarn-overs radiate from a central point like spider legs, with compensating decreases surrounding the centre to maintain stitch count. The motif creates a small circular design resembling a spider or flower.
A length of smooth waste yarn threaded through all live stitches at a given row. Insert one every 40 rows without fail in cobweb-weight lace.

This is the most demanding project in the collection: cobweb weight at 2.5 mm on approximately 720 rows. The spider lace has a 10-stitch, 20-row repeat. One 20-row repeat produces approximately 4 mm of length. Budget about 100 g (about 1,600 m / 1,750 yards) of 1-ply cobweb Shetland-type wool.
What you need

items.name: Needles

items.name: Smooth cotton waste yarn
items.qty: For lifelines every 40 rows — must be very fine to thread through cobweb stitches

content.text: Gauge

36 stitches and 48 rows to 10 cm over spider lace on 2.5 mm needles, blocked. At gauge the 126-stitch cast-on (12 × 10-stitch repeats + 6 selvedge) gives approximately 35 cm width. The 150 cm length requires approximately 720 pattern rows (48 rows per 10 cm × 15 = 720).
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast on

Using the long-tail cast-on over two needles held together, cast on 126 stitches (3 selvedge + 12 × 10-stitch spider repeats + 3 selvedge). Tail: approximately (2.5 × 126) / 10 + 15 = 46.5 cm. Remove one needle after the cast-on.
Spider lace (10 sts, 20 rows)
Work a 3-stitch garter selvedge on each short end throughout. Body stitches (120):

RS Row 1: *k1, yo, ssk, k4, k2tog, yo; repeat from *. RS Row 3: *k2, yo, ssk, k2, k2tog, yo, k1; repeat from *. RS Row 5: *k3, yo, k3tog, yo, k2; repeat from * (creates spider centre). RS Row 7: *k2, k2tog, yo, k1, yo, ssk, k1; repeat from *. RS Row 9: *k1, k2tog, yo, k3, yo, ssk; repeat from *. WS rows (even): k3 selvedge, p to last 3 sts, k3 selvedge. Work rows 11 to 20 as a mirror of rows 1 to 10 to complete the spider.
Continue the 20-row repeat until the stole measures 150 cm long. Work 6 garter rows before binding off.
Bind off
Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off. At cobweb weight the bind-off must be worked very loosely to match the elasticity of the cast-on edge.
Common faults

Spider centres misaligned: the k3tog did not sit at the exact spider centre position. The k3tog must sit at stitch 5 of every 10-stitch repeat (the exact centre). Use stitch markers to mark every repeat boundary.
Yarn breaking at the k3tog: cobweb weight is fragile. Work the k3tog slowly and support the three stitches from below with a finger while passing the right needle through.
Blocking

Soak 30 minutes in cool water. The blocked stole must be held under its own weight for 48 hours to fully dry. Pin to 35 × 150 cm with extremely close pins (every 2 cm) along both long edges to hold the spider motifs open. Use a pin at every spider centre point.
Care
Hand wash with extreme care in cool water, since 1-ply yarn breaks if agitated. Roll in a dry towel, do not wring. Lay flat to dry. Re-block after every wear.
What to try next
Add a knitted-on Shetland edging along both long edges. Pick up one stitch per selvedge row. Work a 12-stitch deep edging cast-off sideways, using a simple zig-zag lace motif.
